title.narrative: UN Global Disability Fund, GDF (f.d. UNPRPD), 2019-2025 (2026)
UN Global Disability Fund, GDF (f.d. UNPRPD), 2019-2025 (2026)

description.narrative:
Mission and vision of the Global Disability Fund The mission of the Global Disability Fund is to support countries in accelerating implementation of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) and the disability-inclusive Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), with the full and meaningful participation of organisations of persons with disabilities (OPDs).
The Fund's vision is a world where every person with disabilities enjoys full and equitable participation in society, with their rights promoted, protected and fulfilled.
Strategic Operational Framework (SOF) 2020-2025 The 2025 Annual Report demonstrates that the UN Global Disability Fund continued to deliver results in line with the Strategic Operational Framework (SOF) 2020-2025 during its final year of implementation. Across 51 countries, the Fund supported governments, public institutions, United Nations entities and organisations of persons with disabilities (OPDs) to strengthen disability-inclusive policies, systems and planning processes through joint UN programmes. The reporting shows continued progress towards strengthening national capacity for CRPD implementation while laying the foundation for the Fund's new Strategy 2025-2030.
The SOF is built around three interrelated outcomes: Outcome 1: National stakeholders are equipped with the knowledge and practical tools for disability-inclusive policies and systems.
Outcome 2: Gaps in achieving the essential building blocks or preconditions to CRPD implementation are addressed.
Outcome 3: National development plans and monitoring processes include disability mainstreaming.
These outcomes are supported through three mutually reinforcing strategic approaches: (i) catalytic funding for national and multi-country joint programmes on disability inclusion; (ii) knowledge management and lessons learned; and (iii) context-relevant capacity building to strengthen disability-inclusive systems and policies in both development and humanitarian contexts.
Global Disability Fund Strategy 2025-2030 The Global Disability Fund Strategy 2025-2030 marks a shift from supporting individual disability-inclusive initiatives towards catalysing long-term, nationally owned systems change. The Fund seeks to move from global commitments to local implementation by strengthening national institutions, policies, financing systems and partnerships that enable implementation of the CRPD and disability-inclusive SDGs.
A defining feature of the Strategy is the transition from consultation to OPD co-leadership. Organisations of persons with disabilities are positioned as partners, decision-makers and implementers, with increased influence over national policies, service delivery and financing. The Fund also expands its financing modalities beyond the UN system, enabling direct support to OPDs, governments and civil society where appropriate.
The strategy is organised around five strategic goals: 1. OPDs Leading the Change - Persons with disabilities, through their representative organisations drive systemic transformation. 2. Essential Services - Equitable access to inclusive health, education, gender-based violence prevention and response, and urban services. 3. Physical & Digital Accessibility - Inclusive infrastructure, information, transport and digital platforms enabling mobility and independence. 4. Support & Protection Services - Inclusive gender-based violence prevention, referral and response, care, and protection systems, especially for women, girls and marginalised persons. 5. Resilience - Inclusive preparedness, response and recovery enabling resilience to climate change, conflicts and humanitarian crises.
Four thematic areas: Priorities for countries The Strategy identifies four thematic priority areas that countries may draw upon depending on national context and priorities: 1. Essential services 2. Climate and Humanitarian Crises 3. Women and girls' health and protection 4. Urban development.
Four pathways of change The strategy outlines four pathways describing how GDF aims to achieve systemic change: 1. Practices: Strengthening inclusive planning, delivery and monitoring within institutions and service providers. 2. Partnerships: Building coordinated and accountable collaboration between governments, UN agencies, OPDs and civil society, centred on OPD leadership. 3. Policies and financing: Embedding disability inclusion into national laws, strategies, budgets and financial systems. 4. Knowledge and learning: Improving data, evidence and adaptive learning through the Results and Learning Framework and Inclusion Catalyst Hub.
Together, these pathways describe how the Fund seeks to move from isolated projects to sustained, system-wide change, supporting nationally owned implementation of the CRPD and disability-inclusive SDGs.

The UN Global Disability Fund (GDF, formerly UNPRPD) is the UN system’s only pooled fund dedicated to strengthening the implementation of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) and advancing systemic inclusion of persons with disabilities. The Fund brings together 14 UN entities, governments and organizations of persons with disabilities (OPDs) to deepen rights-based inclusion through joint programmes and nationally owned reforms.
The GDF Strategy 2025–2030 is grounded in rights-based approaches, gender equality integration and OPD leadership, alongside strengthened accountability mechanisms. It also aims to contribute to inclusive resilience, accessible reconstruction and disability-inclusive crisis management systems, including in contexts such as Ukraine.
GDF is a central actor in driving long-term reforms in accessibility, inclusive services, protection systems and resilience. The Fund works to strengthen disability inclusion across the UN system and is mandated to support the implementation of the UN Disability Inclusion Strategy (UN-DIS), adopted by the UN Secretary-General in 2019.
Sida is a long-standing donor, providing annual support of approximately 27–30 MSEK. The contribution is provided as core support through a multilaterally managed pooled fund (UNDP/MPTFO), enabling coordinated UN action, national policy development, institutional capacity strengthening and enhanced OPD leadership, in line with OECD/DAC definitions of pooled funding and technical assistance for governance and rights implementation.

UN Global Disability Fund (GDF, tidigare UNPRPD) är FN-systemets enda gemensamma fond för att stärka genomförandet av konventionen om rättigheter för personer med funktionsnedsättning (CRPD) och driva systemisk inkludering av personer med funktionsnedsättning. Fonden samlar 14 FN-organ, regeringar och organisationer av personer med funktionsnedsättning (OPDs) för att genom gemensamma program och nationellt ägda reformer fördjupa rättighetsbaserad inkludering.
GDF:s strategi 2025–2030 bygger på rättighetsbaserade ansatser, jämställdhetsintegrering och OPD-ledarskap samt stärkta ansvarsmekanismer, men syftar även att bidra till inkluderande resiliens, tillgänglighet i återuppbyggnad och inkluderande krishanteringssystem i exempelvis Ukraina.
GDF är en central aktör för att driva långsiktiga förändringar inom tillgänglighet, inkluderande tjänster, skyddssystem och motståndskraft. GDF arbetar för att stärka integrering av funktionshinderperspektiv i FN-systemet och har ett mandat att stödja genomförandet av FN:s strategi för integrering av funktionshinderperspektivet (UN-DIS) som antogs av FN:s generalsekreterare 2019.
Sida är en långvarig givare med ett årligt stöd på omkring 27-30 MSEK. Stödet ges som kärnstöd via en multilateralt förvaltad pool-fond (UNDP/MPTFO). Detta möjliggör samordnad FN-insats, nationell policyutveckling, institutionell kapacitetsförstärkning och stärkt OPD-ledarskap i linje med OECD/DAC:s definitioner av pooled funding och tekniskt stöd inom styrning och rättighetsimplementering.

The reported results are presented below according to the three outcomes of the Strategic Operational Framework (SOF) 20202025, which remained the Fund's governing results framework throughout the reporting period. Although 2025 marked the first year of implementation of the Global Disability Fund Strategy 20252030, the reported achievements primarily reflect progress against the objectives of the SOF. Together, the examples illustrate how country-level programmes contributed to institutional and systems-level change across the Fund's three intended outcomes.
Outcome 1: National stakeholders are equipped with the knowledge and practical tools for disability-inclusive policies and systems. During 2025, the Fund continued strengthening the capacity of governments, United Nations Country Teams and organisations of persons with disabilities (OPDs) to develop and implement disability-inclusive policies and systems. Across the portfolio, programmes combined technical assistance, practical implementation tools and institutional capacity development, demonstrating continued progress in translating CRPD commitments into institutional practice. Examples of results include:
- In Cambodia, more than 4,500 stakeholders strengthened their capacity to design and implement disability-inclusive policies and services, with 87 percent reporting improved knowledge and skills following training and technical support.
- In Eswatini, disability indicators were integrated into the national Health Management Information System (HMIS) and Education Management Information System (EMIS), while more than 300 health professionals were trained in neonatal disability screening.
- In Guatemala, government institutions, municipalities and OPDs jointly developed disability-inclusive planning tools, accessibility standards and disability data systems to support more inclusive public planning and service delivery.
The Accelerating Disability Rights in Cambodia programme illustrates these results particularly well. In addition to large-scale capacity development, the programme strengthened six Provincial Disability Action Councils and established 18 District Disability Action Councils, contributing to stronger local ownership and increased budget allocations for disability inclusion. As a result, access to inclusive services increased from 4,995 persons with disabilities in 2021 to 46,487 in 2025, demonstrating how strengthened institutional capacity translated into improved service delivery.
Outcome 2: Gaps in achieving the essential building blocks or preconditions to CRPD implementation are addressed. The reporting demonstrates continued progress in strengthening the policy, governance and institutional foundations required for implementation of the CRPD. Across 36 country programmes, the Fund contributed to 98 regulatory and systems changes, while 22 countries established or strengthened formal mechanisms for OPD participation. In total, 1,323 stakeholders participated in the design, reform and implementation of disability-inclusive policies and systems. Examples of results include:
- In Zimbabwe, the Government operationalised the National Disability Policy through a costed Action Plan, disability-inclusive budgeting tools and strengthened public oversight.
- In Ecuador, the national manual for sexual and reproductive health and gender-based violence services was revised to align with CRPD standards through close collaboration with the Ministry of Health and organisations of persons with disabilities.
- In Fiji, technical assistance supported review of employment legislation and development of proposals to strengthen protection against disability-based discrimination in the labour market.
Zimbabwe provides a good example of how policy and institutional reforms can translate into improved public services for persons with disabilities. GDF supported implementation of the National Disability Policy through a costed Action Plan, disability-inclusive budgeting tools and new auditing guidelines adopted by the Office of the Auditor General. Building on these reforms, integrated one-stop centres and mobile outreach services improved access to gender-based violence services for more than 550 women and girls with disabilities during 2025, illustrating how stronger governance and financing systems can lead to better services for rights-holders.
Outcome 3: National development plans and monitoring processes include disability mainstreaming. Disability inclusion became increasingly integrated into national development planning and monitoring during 2025. Across the portfolio, 25 countries advanced disability-inclusive UN development and humanitarian programming, 31 countries strengthened disability-inclusive national development planning for the SDGs, and 39 countries established or reinforced formal mechanisms enabling organisations of persons with disabilities (OPDs) to participate in national planning and monitoring processes. Examples of results include:
- In Ghana, the Government established a National Disability Database and operationalised a National Disability Data Framework to strengthen disability-inclusive planning and SDG monitoring.
- In Mozambique, disability inclusion was incorporated into the Common Country Analysis for the first time, providing an evidence base for the next United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework.
- In Kenya, OPDs participated in county budget consultations for the 2025/26 planning cycle, contributing to disability-inclusive budgeting, humanitarian preparedness and emergency planning.
- Across ten Pacific Island countries, governments, UN agencies and OPDs strengthened disability-inclusive planning through regional cooperation, technical assistance and peer learning.
Ghana demonstrates well how stronger national systems can support disability-inclusive development planning. The Government developed a National Disability Database and operationalised a National Disability Data Framework, both linked to the national statistical platform, StatsBank. This strengthened the use of disability-disaggregated data in national planning and enabled disability indicators to be more systematically reflected in Ghana's Voluntary National Review of the SDGs. A multi-stakeholder workshop involving 65 representatives from government, OPDs, civil society and the United Nations further strengthened coordination around disability-inclusive development planning.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
